items.stem: Define the term 'hard HRM'.
items.answer: An approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible, with a focus on cost control, short-term contracts and close monitoring.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, an approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible, with a focus on cost control, short-term contracts and close monitoring. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between hard HRM and soft HRM.
items.answer: Hard HRM treats workers as a cost to be minimised and controlled; soft HRM treats them as assets to be developed, consulted and motivated for the long term.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hard; 1 mark soft. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a business facing strong price competition might adopt a hard HRM approach.
items.answer: It must keep unit labour costs low, so it matches staffing to demand, uses flexible contracts and controls pay closely.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cost pressure; 1 mark hard methods used. [2]

items.stem: Based in Mumbai, Deccan Auto Components Ltd (public limited company) supplies brakes and steering parts to car manufacturers. The business has around 2,200 employees. Its car-maker customers are switching rapidly to electric vehicles. Explain how Deccan Auto could benefit from moving from a hard to a soft HRM approach.
items.answer: Points to develop for Deccan Auto: soft HRM treats staff as assets; training raises productivity and quality of brake and steering components; involvement increases motivation (e.g. Herzberg motivators); lower labour turnover cuts recruitment costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: soft HRM treats staff as assets. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Deccan Auto: automotive components, about 2,200 employees, public limited company in India; its car-maker customers are switching rapidly to electric vehicles). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Deccan Auto, e.g. training raises productivity and quality of brake and steering components; involvement increases motivation (e.g. Herzberg motivators); lower labour turnover cuts recruitment costs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: World cocoa prices have doubled in eighteen months. Gold Coast Cocoa Ltd, a private limited company in Ghana with about 450 employees, buys cocoa from local co-operatives and makes premium chocolate bars. Explain how workforce planning could help Gold Coast Cocoa achieve its objectives.
items.answer: Points to develop for Gold Coast Cocoa: workforce planning forecasts labour demand and supply; identifies skills gaps before they cause problems; plans recruitment, training or redeployment; controls labour costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: workforce planning forecasts labour demand and supply. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Gold Coast Cocoa: confectionery, about 450 employees, private limited company in Ghana; world cocoa prices have doubled in eighteen months). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Gold Coast Cocoa, e.g. identifies skills gaps before they cause problems; plans recruitment, training or redeployment; controls labour costs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd is a private limited company based in Cape Town, South Africa. It brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets and employs about 140 people. Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. Evaluate whether Cape Brew should adopt a soft rather than a hard approach to HRM.
items.answer: For: motivated, loyal staff; better quality and innovation; lower turnover. Against: higher costs of training and consultation; competitive pressure on costs; some roles suit flexible contracts. Judgement: the decision for Cape Brew depends mainly on the skills its staff need, and also on its competitive strategy (cost or differentiation).
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Cape Brew: beverages, about 140 employees, private limited company in South Africa; demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. motivated, loyal staff; better quality and innovation; lower turnover; arguments against, e.g. higher costs of training and consultation; competitive pressure on costs; some roles suit flexible contracts. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the skills its staff need; its competitive strategy (cost or differentiation); its corporate culture. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Cape Brew, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Pearl Logistics WLL is a private limited company based in Doha, Qatar. It provides freight forwarding, warehousing and lorry delivery services and employs about 1,500 people. Large customers are asking for real-time tracking of every delivery. Using the case and your own knowledge, discuss the importance of workforce planning for Pearl Logistics over the next five years.
items.answer: For: avoids skills shortages; controls labour costs; supports growth plans. Against: forecasts may be inaccurate; labour market changes quickly; flexible contracts can fill gaps. Judgement: the decision for Pearl Logistics depends mainly on how fast the business grows, and also on the availability of skilled labour in Qatar.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO4 Evaluation [5]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on how fast the business grows; the availability of skilled labour in Qatar; the quality of its data. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Pearl Logistics, not a generic one. [16]

items.stem: Which policy is most closely associated with soft HRM?
options: Long-term training and career development for all staff
Using short-term contracts to cut costs
items.answer: Long-term training and career development for all staff
items.markingKey: Long-term training and career development for all staff. Soft HRM sees staff as assets to be developed and involved.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'workforce planning'?
options: Analysing the current workforce and forecasting the number and skills of employees the business will need in future, then planning how to meet the gap.
The percentage of possible working days lost through staff absence: days lost ÷ total possible working days × 100.
A method of resolving industrial disputes in which an independent third party (e.g. ACAS) helps both sides talk and reach their own agreement.
An approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible, with a focus on cost control, short-term contracts and close monitoring.
items.answer: Analysing the current workforce and forecasting the number and skills of employees the business will need in future, then planning how to meet the gap.
items.markingKey: workforce planning: Analysing the current workforce and forecasting the number and skills of employees the business will need in future, then planning how to meet the gap.

items.stem: Explain two benefits of workforce planning to a growing business.
items.answer: It identifies future skill shortages early so recruitment and training can be planned; it avoids over- or under-staffing and the costs they cause.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark benefit, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'zero-hours contract'.
items.answer: An employment contract under which the employer does not guarantee any minimum number of hours, and the worker is paid only for hours actually worked.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, an employment contract under which the employer does not guarantee any minimum number of hours, and the worker is paid only for hours actually worked. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why zero-hours contracts may reduce employee motivation.
items.answer: Uncertain hours and income threaten security needs (Maslow), so workers feel less valued and less committed, and may leave when they find secure work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark insecurity of income/hours; 1 mark link to motivation theory or turnover. [2]

items.stem: Explain one benefit to a business of using gig-economy workers rather than permanent employees.
items.answer: It pays only for completed tasks and avoids costs such as holiday pay and pensions, so costs fall and it can scale up or down quickly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Café Cordillera SAS is a private limited company based in Bogotá, Colombia. It roasts coffee and runs a chain of 60 cafés and employs about 900 people. The owners want to double the number of cafés within three years. Explain the possible effects on employees and customers if Café Cordillera moves many staff onto zero-hours contracts.
items.answer: Points to develop for Café Cordillera: zero-hours contracts give no guaranteed hours; insecurity lowers motivation and loyalty; higher turnover may reduce service quality; customers may react to reputational damage.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: zero-hours contracts give no guaranteed hours. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Café Cordillera: food and drink retail, about 900 employees, private limited company in Colombia; the owners want to double the number of cafés within three years). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Café Cordillera, e.g. insecurity lowers motivation and loyalty; higher turnover may reduce service quality; customers may react to reputational damage. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.answer: Points to develop for Nile Pharma: flexibility matches labour to demand; lower labour cost per unit of output; multi-skilled staff cover absences; faster response to changes in demand for generic medicines.

items.answer: Permanent $200,000; zero-hours $138,000

items.stem: Define the term 'labour turnover'.
items.answer: The percentage of a firm's workforce that leaves during a year: number leaving ÷ average number employed × 100.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, the percentage of a firm's workforce that leaves during a year: number leaving ÷ average number employed × 100. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a high rate of absenteeism may indicate a problem with motivation.
items.answer: Workers who are dissatisfied or stressed are more likely to take days off; Herzberg's hygiene factors (conditions, supervision) may be poor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link to dissatisfaction; 1 mark cause/theory. [2]

items.stem: Explain why some labour turnover can benefit a business.
items.answer: New staff bring fresh ideas and skills, and leavers can be replaced with lower-paid or better-matched recruits, or not replaced if cutting costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'trade union'.
items.answer: An organisation of workers that aims to protect and improve its members' pay, conditions and job security through collective action.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, an organisation of workers that aims to protect and improve its members' pay, conditions and job security through collective action. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain one benefit to an employer of negotiating with a trade union rather than with individual employees.
items.answer: Collective bargaining saves time and cost because one agreement covers many workers, and union representatives communicate decisions to members.
items.markingKey: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between conciliation and arbitration.
items.answer: In conciliation a third party helps the two sides reach their own agreement; in arbitration the third party decides the outcome.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: At Muscat Dates & Co. LLC, 300 unionised workers are each paid $18,000 a year. The union claims a 6% pay rise; management offers 3%. items.stem: Explain the difference between numerical flexibility and functional flexibility.
items.answer: Numerical flexibility changes the number of workers or hours (e.g. temporary, part-time staff); functional flexibility means existing staff can perform different tasks.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'zero-hours contract'?

An employment contract under which the employer does not guarantee any minimum number of hours, and the worker is paid only for hours actually worked.
A labour market in which many people work on short-term, task-by-task contracts, often arranged through online platforms, rather than in permanent jobs.
An approach that treats employees as valuable assets whose commitment is developed through training, involvement, consultation and long-term career development.
items.answer: An employment contract under which the employer does not guarantee any minimum number of hours, and the worker is paid only for hours actually worked.
